parts.partTitle: Why Getters & Setters Break Your Code

beats.headline: Is your code an anemic bag of getters?
beats.subline: Public fields and blind setters are the primary cause of fragile, unmaintainable domain models.
beats.narration: If you mark every field private but expose every single setter, you have zero encapsulation. You are just creating an anemic model where domain logic leaks into every service class.

beats.title: Anemic vs. Behavior-Focused

top.label: Anemic (Bad)

bottom.label: Encapsulated (Good)

beats.narration: Stop asking objects for their state to modify it externally. Tell the object what to do. By moving logic inside the class, you guarantee that the object remains in a valid state.

beats.title: The Tell-Don't-Ask Pattern

steps.explanation: Private helper method ensures the account isn't frozen before any operation runs.
Validates inputs immediately, preventing the object from ever entering an invalid state.

beats.narration: This is real encapsulation. The class guards its own invariants. If the account is frozen or the withdrawal amount is invalid, the object rejects the operation before it even touches the data.

beats.title: Information Hiding Strategy
beats.subtitle: Hide the how, expose the what
beats.narration: Information hiding means callers only depend on your public methods. You can change your internal storage from double to BigDecimal or long cents, and zero external code will break.

beats.narration: That is the core of encapsulation. In Part 2, we dissect the four access modifiers and the subtle traps of protected inheritance.

beats.headline: Why is protected actually dangerous?
beats.subline: It isn't just 'package-private plus'. It creates a permanent API contract for subclasses.
beats.narration: Most developers think protected is just a slightly wider package-private. It is actually a massive design commitment that exposes your internals to any subclass in the entire application.

beats.title: The Visibility Hierarchy
beats.subtitle: Narrower is always safer
beats.narration: Start with private. Use package-private for internal collaborators. Only use protected if you explicitly design your class to be extended, because you cannot easily change it later.

beats.title: The Protected Trap

steps.explanation: You can access protected members on your own instance.
You cannot reach into a parent instance's protected members from a different package.

beats.narration: This is the classic protected trap. You can access protected members on your own subclass instance, but you cannot reach into a parent instance from another package. It is a common source of confusion.

beats.title: Package-Private Organization
beats.caption: Structure your modules

lines.text: # Everything except Service is hidden from other packages

beats.narration: Package-private is your best friend for modularity. Keep your internal collaborators package-private, and only expose the service class. It shrinks your public API surface and makes refactoring painless.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Why immutability is the ultimate encapsulation →
beats.narration: Visibility is about controlling your footprint. In Part 3, we dive into immutability—the ultimate way to protect your object state from accidental corruption.

beats.headline: Is your object actually immutable?
beats.subline: A final field doesn't mean your object is safe. It only means the reference can't change.
beats.narration: If you have a final list field, you aren't safe. Callers can still call dot add on that list. True immutability requires defensive copying and unmodifiable views.

beats.title: The Immutability Checklist

steps.explanation: Prevents subclasses from overriding methods to introduce mutability.
List.copyOf creates an unmodifiable, deep-ish copy that protects against external changes.

beats.narration: To be truly immutable, the class must be final, fields must be private and final, and you must defensively copy mutable inputs. List dot copyOf is your best friend here.

beats.title: Why Immutability Matters
beats.narration: Mutable objects as map keys are a recipe for disaster. If the hashcode changes, your data vanishes. Immutable objects are inherently thread-safe and make your code significantly easier to reason about.

beats.title: Modern Records (Java 16+)

steps.explanation: Automatically generates final fields, constructor, and accessors.
Crucial: always defensively copy mutable components here.

beats.narration: Records are perfect for data carriers. But remember, they are only shallowly immutable. You must still defensively copy mutable components like lists in the compact constructor.

beats.headline: Can you refactor without breaking callers?
beats.subline: Encapsulation isn't just about syntax. It is the key to building systems that evolve over years, not months.
beats.narration: If your code is hard to change, you have failed at encapsulation. It is the architectural foundation that allows you to refactor internals while keeping your public contracts stable.

beats.title: The Encapsulation Checklist
beats.subtitle: Review your classes against these rules
beats.narration: Follow this checklist. Default to private, guard your invariants inside the class, and use immutability to prevent accidental state corruption. This is how you build production-grade Java.
